title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated feedback on student writing can be used effectively in higher education language learning, and whether students prefer it to feedback from human tutors. The authors focus on the emerging use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4, as an automated writing evaluation tool for English as a new language (ENL) learners. The study addresses two core questions: whether AI feedback produces stronger writing gains than human feedback, and whether students prefer AI-generated or tutor-generated feedback.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted over six weeks. In Study 1, the intervention compared GPT-4-generated writing feedback with feedback from human tutors in a repeated-measures quasi-experimental design. ENL students completed weekly 300-word academic writing tasks, received either AI or human feedback, revised their work, and were assessed through pre- and post-writing tests scored with an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a separate group of students received both AI-generated and human tutor feedback on weekly assignments, then completed weekly surveys with Likert-scale and open-ended items about satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference.

The population consisted of 91 ENL university students enrolled in an academic reading and writing course at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. Study 1 included 48 students, and Study 2 included 43 different students. Human tutors were trained English language tutors from the university’s ENL Tutor Program, while GPT-4 feedback was generated using an iteratively developed prompt designed by experienced language educators. The intervention occurred in the context of regular course writing assignments during a shortened Spring 2023 semester.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated feedback did not produce significantly different writing gains compared with human tutor feedback. Students in both conditions improved similarly over the six-week period. Preference data showed an almost even split between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred human tutors valued face-to-face interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask immediate follow-up questions, while those preferring AI valued clarity, specificity, consistency, and detailed academic language suggestions. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback can likely be incorporated into ENL writing instruction without harming learning outcomes, and they recommend a blended approach that combines the efficiency and specificity of AI with the interpersonal benefits of human tutoring.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot interface used here with GPT-family models to generate automated writing evaluation feedback on student essays.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an automated writing evaluation tool to provide GPT-4-generated corrective feedback on weekly ENL student writing, compared against feedback from human tutors and evaluated for learner outcomes and student preference.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1, ENL students who received ChatGPT/GPT-4-generated writing feedback showed no significant difference in writing improvement compared with students who received human tutor feedback over a six-week quasi-experimental repeated-measures design. The group × time interaction was not significant (F=3.094, p=0.085, ηp²=0.063), and the between-subjects group effect was also not significant (F=0.241, p=0.626, ηp²=0.005); sample size was n=48 total (EG n=23, CG n=25).
findings.measure: Pre/post analytic writing rubric scores assessing content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2, student preference between ChatGPT/GPT-4 feedback and human tutor feedback was nearly evenly split among ENL learners. On the forced-choice preference item, the six-week grand mean was 1.53 (SD=0.5) where 1 indicated preference for human feedback and 2 indicated preference for AI feedback; average weekly counts were 18 preferring human feedback versus 19.667 preferring AI feedback, with weekly responses ranging from n=32 to n=41 (43 participants overall).
findings.measure: Weekly preference survey on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, overall preference, and forced-choice feedback preference

findings.finding_summary: Students generally rated both ChatGPT/GPT-4 and human tutor feedback positively, with all grand means for survey items above 4 except none falling below 4 except week-specific dips for Q6 and Q8 in week 2. Across six weeks, AI feedback grand means were satisfaction 4.26, clarity 4.24, helpfulness 4.23, and preference 4.13, slightly below corresponding human tutor means of 4.28, 4.32, 4.31, and 4.20, suggesting both were valued with a slight edge for human feedback on averaged Likert ratings.
findings.measure: Likert-scale student perceptions of satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference

quality_tier_rationale: The paper reports two empirical longitudinal studies, including a repeated-measures quasi-experimental design with a comparison group for learning outcomes, but it is not a randomized trial and uses self-selected participants from a single university context.
impact_tier_rationale: The main efficacy result found no significant difference in writing outcomes between ChatGPT-generated and human tutor feedback, and preference results were essentially split with only slight descriptive differences.
